Women Disciples
WIM-in dih-SY-puhlz
noun
From women + disciple; the faithful women who followed and ministered to Christ and the apostles.

📖 Biblical Definition

The women disciples were the company of faithful women who followed the Lord Jesus, ministered to Him of their substance, stood by His cross when the men had fled, watched the sepulchre, and were the first witnesses of His resurrection. Luke names Mary called Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, and many others, who followed Him out of Galilee and ministered unto Him of their substance (Luke 8:2-3). They followed Him to Calvary and beheld where He was laid; and to them first the risen Christ appeared, sending them to tell His brethren—so that women carried the first word of the resurrection to the apostles. In the early church, women such as Mary the mother of John Mark, Lydia, Priscilla, Dorcas, and Phoebe served Christ in prayer, hospitality, instruction of women, works of mercy, and the support of the gospel. Scripture honors their devotion without overturning the order God appointed: the office of elder is reserved to qualified men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7), while the labors of godly women are essential, honored, and dear to Christ. The dictionary celebrates the women disciples as a chief glory of the gospel—last at the cross, first at the tomb—and rebukes both the world that despises them and the error that would erase the order in which their service shines.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The faithful women who followed and ministered to Christ; last at the cross, first at the tomb, and witnesses of the resurrection, honored within God’s appointed order.

WOMEN DISCIPLES, the faithful women who followed and ministered to Christ.

Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, and many others ministered of their substance.

Stood by the cross when the men had fled; watched the sepulchre.

First witnesses of the resurrection, sent to tell the apostles.

Honored within God’s order: eldership reserved to qualified men (1Ti 2:12).

📖 Key Scripture

Luk 8:3 — "And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance."

Mat 27:55 — "And many women were there beholding afar off, which followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him:"

Joh 20:18 — "Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had spoken these things unto her."

Rom 16:1 — "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The women disciples are seized by egalitarians to overturn male eldership and dismissed by others as marginal; Scripture honors them within the order God set.

expand to see more

The corruption to resist is the egalitarian seizure of the women disciples as a proof-text against the order God has appointed. Because faithful women followed Christ, ministered to Him, and first announced His resurrection, the argument runs that male-only eldership must fall. But devotion and office are not the same thing. The Lord who was served by these women is the same Lord whose apostle, writing by the Spirit, reserves the teaching-and-ruling office of elder to qualified men (1 Tim 2:12; 3:1-7). To honor the women disciples is not to erase that order but to see their service shine within it.

The opposite corruption despises or marginalizes these women, as though their service were a lesser footnote. Scripture does the reverse: it records that they stood by the cross when the men had fled (Matt 27:55), that the risen Christ appeared first to them and sent them to the apostles (John 20:18), and that women like Phoebe were commended servants of the church (Rom 16:1). The dictionary celebrates the women disciples without adopting the egalitarian framing, and recovers the truth that God’s order and the honor of godly women are not enemies but friends—the order is the very setting in which their devotion is most beautiful.

Women + disciple; the faithful women who followed and ministered to Christ, honored as witnesses of the resurrection within God’s appointed order.
